newsitem.title: CHINA: Rule changes seen boosting China car market.
newsitem.headline: Rule changes seen boosting China car market.

text.p: Rule changes and a recent cut in interest rates could boost China's flagging car market, but rampant smuggling and official restrictions are likely to keep legal imports down, the China Daily Business Weekly said on Sunday.

Sales of imported cars slumped to 35,700 units in the first half of the year, down 30 percent from the same period of 1995, but a recent ban on local restrictions on economy cars was expected to help revive imports, the official newspaper said.

The market could also be boosted as Chinese enterprises began to feel the benefit of an August cut in interest rates, it quoted Chen Ping, vice president of the China National Automotive Trading Corp, as saying.
Sales would continue to be sluggish until the end of the year, partly due to surviving local restrictions that dampened car buyers' enthusiasm, Chen said but gave no details.
Many local authorities levy a bewildering number of fees and charges on the sale and use of new cars.
Chen said smuggling continued to make it difficult to sell officially imported cars, which are subject to hefty tariffs that can more than double their cost.
Japanese customs figures put January-June car exports to China at 20,000 vehicles, but China's customs statistics recorded only 9,000 units -- suggesting many were smuggled into the country, he said.

Foreign and domestic producers have rushed to position themselves in China, seen by many as the world's largest potential car market, but slumping sales and fierce competition have disappointed automakers.

Chinese media reported on Friday that Beijing had banned restrictions on economy cars as part of a move to clamp down on regional protectionism that industry experts say is hampering development of the national market.

China produced 1.5 million motor vehicles in 1995 and is expected to manufacture 2.7 million in the year 2000. The registered car population is forecast to double to 20 million by the year 2000 from around 10 million in 1996.
